result.summary: Pausanias describes Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, its juniper-wood statue of Hermes and its white blackbirds, then turns to Mount Chelydorea. He ends with the road from Pheneus to Nonacris and the water of the Styx.

scenes.title: Mount Cyllene and its white blackbirds
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Cyllene, its ruined temple, the juniper statue of Hermes and the white blackbirds, comparing other white animals he has seen.

scenes.title: Chelydorea and the tortoise
scenes.summary: The neighbouring mountain Chelydorea is where Hermes is said to have found the tortoise and made a lyre.

scenes.title: Road to Nonacris and the Styx
scenes.summary: From Pheneus the roads lead to Clitor and to ruined Nonacris, near a high cliff dripping the water called the Styx.

analysis.text: Pausanias links landscape, cult and myth, explaining names by local heroes and gods and reporting marvels like white blackbirds.
His comparisons with white animals and his personal observations show the travel-writer's method of eyewitness checking.

legacy.text: The tale of Hermes making a lyre from a tortoise shell is told in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes and became a lasting image in art.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says the Cyllenian Hermes statue was of juniper wood, unusual among the woods used for early statues.

language_notes.text: "Got their title" means the mountain and the god received the name Cyllenian from Cyllen, a local figure.
"Lodge" means roost or dwell; the blackbirds are said to live on the mountain permanently.
Pausanias distinguishes the Bœotian birds sharing the name blackbird; they are not songbirds, unlike the white ones.
"Swan-eagles" is the popular name for a white eagle that looked like a swan.
Refers to the myth that the infant Hermes killed a tortoise and strung its shell with strings to make the first lyre.
The Styx was the water by which gods swore their most binding oaths; this Arcadian stream was identified with it.

context_notes.text: Juniper was an aromatic, durable wood, so a juniper statue was an archaic and unusual cult image.
Lycaon was a legendary early king of Arcadia, whose wife gave Nonacris its name.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias presents himself as a widely travelled eyewitness, building his authority by listing white animals he has personally seen.
His claim that he recalls no higher cliff stresses the Styx's awe-inspiring setting, though it is framed as personal experience.
